claims.lossDescription: A pan of oil caught fire on the stovetop. The fire burned the kitchen cabinets and smoke stained the walls of the kitchen and dining room.
claims.question: Is the fire and smoke damage to the dwelling covered?
claims.reasoning: Coverage A covers the dwelling against direct physical loss unless excluded (I.PERILS.A.1). Fire and smoke are not excluded.

claims.lossDescription: During a cold snap a pipe in the exterior wall of the upstairs bathroom froze and burst. The furnace was running and the house was heated. Water soaked the ceiling of the room below.
claims.question: Is the water damage to the ceiling covered?
claims.reasoning: Freezing is excluded under I.PERILS.A.2.b only if the insured failed to use reasonable care to maintain heat. Heat was maintained, so the loss is covered under open perils.

claims.lossDescription: During heavy rain, water backed up through the floor drain in the basement and soaked the carpet and the lower drywall.
claims.question: Is the damage to the basement carpet and drywall covered?
claims.reasoning: Water that backs up through sewers or drains is excluded by I.EXCL.3.b. HO-1001 has no water backup endorsement.

claims.lossDescription: Burglars broke a back window and stole a jewelry box containing a diamond bracelet worth $4,000. A police report was filed.
claims.question: Is the theft of the bracelet covered?
claims.reasoning: Theft is a Coverage C peril (I.PERILS.C.9), so the loss is covered, but the special limit for theft of jewelry (I.C.3.e) caps payment at $1,500 for all jewelry in the loss.

claims.lossDescription: A gold bracelet slipped off the insured's wrist while swimming at a public beach and could not be found. Nobody took it.
claims.question: Is the lost bracelet covered?
claims.reasoning: Personal property is covered only for the perils listed under Coverage C (I.PERILS.C.0). Losing an item is not one of them, and the theft peril (I.PERILS.C.9) requires that the property was likely stolen.

claims.lossDescription: An earthquake cracked the foundation and several interior walls of the dwelling.
claims.question: Is the earthquake damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Earth movement, including earthquake, is excluded by I.EXCL.2.

claims.lossDescription: An earthquake broke the gas line to the water heater, and the escaping gas caught fire and burned the utility room and kitchen.
claims.question: Is the fire damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Earth movement is excluded, but I.EXCL.2 says direct loss by fire resulting from earth movement is covered. The fire damage is covered; damage done by the shaking itself is not.

claims.lossDescription: A windstorm tore shingles and sheathing off part of the roof. Rain came in through the opening and damaged the bedroom ceiling and a wooden dresser.
claims.question: Is the damage to the ceiling and the dresser covered?
claims.reasoning: The ceiling is part of the dwelling, covered for any direct physical loss not excluded (I.PERILS.A.1). The dresser is personal property; windstorm (I.PERILS.C.2) covers rain damage inside a building when wind first made an opening in the roof, which it did.

claims.lossDescription: A windstorm blew over a large oak tree in the back yard. It fell across the lawn without hitting any structure or blocking the driveway.
claims.question: Is the cost to replace the tree, or to remove it, covered?
claims.reasoning: Trees are covered only for the perils listed in I.ADD.3, and windstorm is not one of them. Tree removal under I.ADD.1.b is paid only when the fallen tree damages a covered structure or blocks a driveway or ramp; this one did neither.

claims.lossDescription: During a kitchen renovation the contractor found that termites had eaten through several floor joists.
claims.question: Is the termite damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Loss caused by insects is not insured under I.PERILS.A.2.g.7.

claims.lossDescription: A guest slipped on the icy front steps of the dwelling and broke a wrist. The guest has medical bills of $3,800.
claims.question: Are the guest's medical bills covered?
claims.reasoning: Coverage F pays necessary medical expenses for a person injured on the insured location with permission, regardless of whether the insured is legally liable (II.F), up to the Coverage F limit of $5,000.

claims.lossDescription: The insured's dog bit a neighbor at a city park. The neighbor needed stitches and is suing the insured.
claims.question: Is the insured covered for the neighbor's suit?
claims.reasoning: Coverage E applies to bodily injury caused by an occurrence (II.E, DEF.12) anywhere, not only on the insured location, and this form has no animal liability exclusion. The insurer must also defend the suit.

claims.lossDescription: The insured's 16-year-old son mows lawns for neighbors and earned about $1,800 in the past year. He has no employees. A stone thrown by his mower injured a neighbor's eye.
claims.question: Is the son's liability for the injury covered?
claims.reasoning: The son is an insured as a resident relative. His mowing is not a business under the definition, because no insured earned more than $3,000 from it (DEF.6.c); even if it were, the business exclusion does not apply to an insured under 21 in an occasional self-employed business with no employees (II.EXCL.6.c).

claims.lossDescription: While visiting a friend, the insured accidentally knocked over and broke the friend's vase, worth $600.
claims.question: Will the policy pay for the friend's vase?
claims.reasoning: Damage to Property of Others (II.ADD.3) pays up to $1,000 for property of others damaged by an insured, whether or not the insured is legally liable.

claims.lossDescription: While the family was away on a two-week vacation, with the house fully furnished, vandals spray-painted the detached garage door.
claims.question: Is the vandalism damage to the garage covered?
claims.reasoning: The vandalism limitation in I.PERILS.A.2.e applies only when the dwelling has been vacant for more than 60 days. A furnished house whose occupants are temporarily away is unoccupied, not vacant (DEF.16), so the garage (I.B.1) is covered.

claims.lossDescription: Mold was found behind the shower tile. The shower pan had been leaking slowly for over a year; the insured had noticed water stains in the room below last summer but did nothing.
claims.question: Is the mold and water damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Mold is not insured (I.PERILS.A.2.f) unless hidden and caused by an accidental discharge, and constant or repeated leakage over weeks or months is not insured (I.PERILS.A.2.g.9) unless unknown to all insureds. The insured knew of the stains.

claims.lossDescription: Lightning struck a tree next to the house. The surge destroyed the television and a desktop computer.
claims.question: Is the damage to the television and computer covered?
claims.reasoning: Lightning is a Coverage C peril (I.PERILS.C.1). The exclusion of electronic components applies only to the peril of artificially generated electrical current (I.PERILS.C.15), and lightning is not artificially generated.

claims.lossDescription: A utility transformer on the street failed and sent a surge through the house wiring. The circuit boards of the television and a computer were destroyed. There was no storm.
claims.question: Is the damage to the television and computer covered?
claims.reasoning: Personal property is covered only for listed perils (I.PERILS.C.0). The applicable peril, artificially generated electrical current (I.PERILS.C.15), excludes loss to electronic components and circuitry.

claims.lossDescription: Children playing indoors knocked a hole through a drywall partition with a hockey stick.
claims.question: Is the damage to the wall covered?
claims.reasoning: Under the open perils form, the dwelling is covered for any direct physical loss not excluded (I.PERILS.A.1). Accidental damage is not excluded.

claims.lossDescription: A brown water stain appeared on the living room ceiling. The insured does not know where the water came from.
claims.question: Is the ceiling damage covered?
claims.reasoning: The answer depends on the cause, which is unknown: a sudden leak from plumbing is covered (I.PERILS.A.3), a roof leak from worn shingles is not (I.PERILS.A.2.g.1). An inspection must find the source.

claims.lossDescription: After a hailstorm the insured's contractor estimated $18,000 to replace the siding. The insurer's adjuster estimated $11,000.
claims.question: Which estimate will the insurer pay?
claims.reasoning: The policy does not set the amount; it provides a process. Either party may demand appraisal (I.COND.6), and the appraisers and umpire decide the amount of loss.

claims.lossDescription: A friend borrowed the insured's ladder and fell while using it at the friend's own house. The friend says the ladder was defective.
claims.question: Will the policy pay the friend's injuries?
claims.reasoning: Coverage E pays damages only if the insured is legally liable (II.E); whether the insured is liable for a defective ladder is a question of fact and law the policy does not settle. Coverage F does not apply because the injury was off the insured location and not caused by the insured's activities.

claims.lossDescription: A hurricane tore part of the roof off and storm surge flooded the ground floor with seawater.
claims.question: Is the hurricane damage covered?
claims.reasoning: The policy settles each cause but not the split: wind damage is covered (I.PERILS.A.1), storm surge is excluded flood (I.EXCL.3.a), and any damage to which surge contributed is excluded regardless of other causes (I.EXCL.A). How much of the damage each caused is a factual question for the adjuster.

claims.lossDescription: During heavy rain, water backed up through the floor drain in the finished basement and soaked the carpet and the lower drywall.
claims.question: Is the damage to the basement carpet and drywall covered?
claims.reasoning: The water backup endorsement covers water that backs up through drains (PS-WB/1) and deletes exclusion 3.b for that coverage (PS-WB/2), up to the $10,000 Water Backup limit (PS-WB/5, Declarations).

claims.lossDescription: A nearby river overflowed its banks. Water entered the basement through the window wells and also came up through the floor drain.
claims.question: Is the basement damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Overflow of a body of water is flood, excluded by I.EXCL.3.a. The water backup endorsement expressly does not cover flood water that enters a drain and backs up (PS-WB/4).

claims.lossDescription: A storm knocked out power to the neighborhood for ten hours. The sump pump stopped, the sump overflowed, and two inches of water covered the basement floor.
claims.question: Is the basement damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Overflow from a sump is covered by the endorsement (PS-WB/1), and the off-premises power failure exclusion does not apply when the overflow results from loss of power to a sump pump (PS-WB/3).

claims.lossDescription: The sump pump had not worked for several months and the insured had not repaired it. During a rainstorm the sump overflowed into the basement.
claims.question: Is the basement damage covered?
claims.reasoning: The endorsement covers only loss not caused by an insured's negligence (PS-WB/1), and failure to maintain a sump pump in working order is negligence (PS-WB/7).

claims.lossDescription: Burglars stole a three-year-old television. A comparable new set costs $1,400; the insurer says the old set's depreciated value is $600.
claims.question: Will the policy pay the cost of a comparable new television rather than the depreciated value?
claims.reasoning: Theft is a covered peril (I.PERILS.C.9). The replacement cost endorsement settles personal property at replacement cost (PS-RC/1); because the loss exceeds $500, the insurer pays actual cash value first and the rest once the set is replaced (PS-RC/4).

claims.lossDescription: A fire in the living room destroyed a 150-year-old grandfather clock.
claims.question: Will the policy pay the cost of a comparable antique clock rather than the clock's actual cash value?
claims.reasoning: Antiques are ineligible for replacement cost under the endorsement (PS-RC/2), so the clock is settled at actual cash value under the base form (I.COND.4.a).

claims.lossDescription: The water heater in the basement rusted through and burst, spilling water across the finished basement.
claims.question: Is the water damage to the finished basement covered?
claims.reasoning: Rust and wear are not insured, but I.PERILS.A.3 covers the water damage that results when they cause a discharge from a household appliance.

claims.lossDescription: The water heater in the basement rusted through and burst, spilling water across the finished basement.
claims.question: Is the cost of a new water heater covered?
claims.reasoning: Loss caused by rust or corrosion is not insured (I.PERILS.A.2.g.3), and I.PERILS.A.3 expressly excludes loss to the appliance from which the water escaped.

claims.lossDescription: After a storm, the basement floor is wet.
claims.question: Is the basement damage covered?
claims.reasoning: It depends on where the water came from: backup through a drain or sump is covered by the endorsement (PS-WB/1); flood or surface water (I.EXCL.3.a) and ground water seeping through the foundation (I.EXCL.3.c) are excluded. The source is not stated.

claims.lossDescription: Water has been dripping from the ceiling under the upstairs bathroom since sometime last month.
claims.question: Is the ceiling damage covered?
claims.reasoning: A sudden discharge from plumbing is covered (I.PERILS.A.3), but repeated leakage over weeks is not unless it was hidden and unknown to all insureds (I.PERILS.A.2.g.9). The source and how long the leak was known are not established.

claims.lossDescription: The insured lent their car to a neighbor, who crashed it.
claims.question: Does this homeowners policy cover the damage to the car?
claims.reasoning: Motor vehicles are property not covered under Coverage C (I.C.4.c). Damage to the car is a matter for auto insurance.

claims.lossDescription: The furnace's blower motor burned out during a cold spell. Repair costs $3,200. No other property was damaged.
claims.question: Is the furnace repair covered?
claims.reasoning: On 2026-02-10 version 1 is in force, without equipment breakdown coverage. Loss caused by mechanical breakdown is not insured (I.PERILS.A.2.g.2).

claims.lossDescription: The furnace's blower motor burned out during a cold spell. Repair costs $3,200. No other property was damaged.
claims.question: Is the furnace repair covered?
claims.reasoning: On 2026-10-25 version 2 is in force and includes equipment breakdown. A burned-out motor is a sudden mechanical breakdown of covered equipment (PS-EB/1, PS-EB/2), and the mechanical breakdown exclusion does not apply to this coverage (PS-EB/4).

claims.lossDescription: Hail damaged the roof. The repair estimate is $6,000.
claims.question: Is the hail damage covered, and which Section I deductible applies?
claims.reasoning: The loss occurred on the last day of version 1, so its $1,000 deductible applies (HO-1003/v1/DEC.deductible, I.COND.2), not the $2,500 deductible that begins on 2026-05-01. Hail damage to the dwelling is covered (I.PERILS.A.1).

claims.lossDescription: Hail damaged the roof. The repair estimate is $2,000.
claims.question: Will the insurer pay anything for the hail damage?
claims.reasoning: The loss occurred on the first day of version 2, whose Section I deductible is $2,500 (HO-1003/v2/DEC.deductible). The insurer pays only the part of the loss above the deductible (I.COND.2), and $2,000 is below it.

claims.lossDescription: Someone used Priya Holm's stolen identity to open two credit cards and ran up $2,800 in charges. She spent $600 on certified mail, notarized affidavits and a day's lost wages to clear her record.
claims.question: Are the $2,800 of fraudulent charges covered?
claims.reasoning: The identity fraud endorsement pays expenses of recovering from the fraud, but expressly does not cover money, goods or services stolen through it (PS-ID/4).

claims.lossDescription: Someone used Priya Holm's stolen identity to open two credit cards and ran up $2,800 in charges. She spent $600 on certified mail, notarized affidavits and a day's lost wages to clear her record.
claims.question: Are the $600 of expenses covered?
claims.reasoning: Certified mail, notarizing and lost wages are covered expenses (PS-ID/3) of an identity fraud discovered in the policy period (PS-ID/2), less the $250 identity fraud deductible (PS-ID/5).

claims.lossDescription: The refrigerator's compressor failed and $400 of food spoiled before it could be repaired.
claims.question: Is the spoiled food covered?
claims.reasoning: Version 2 includes equipment breakdown, which pays up to $500 for food spoiled by a breakdown of the refrigerator (PS-EB/7).

claims.lossDescription: The refrigerator's compressor failed and $400 of food spoiled before it could be repaired.
claims.question: Is the spoiled food covered?
claims.reasoning: Version 1 has no equipment breakdown coverage. Food is personal property, covered only for the listed Coverage C perils (I.PERILS.C.0), and mechanical failure of a refrigerator is not one of them.

claims.lossDescription: While the family was away for the holidays with the thermostat set at 55°F, a pipe in an outside wall froze and burst, flooding the kitchen.
claims.question: Is the water damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Freezing is excluded only if the insured failed to use reasonable care to maintain heat (I.PERILS.A.2.b). The heat was on, so the loss is covered.

claims.lossDescription: The roof of the detached workshop caved in under the weight of heavy snow. The workshop cannot be used.
claims.question: Is the workshop collapse covered?
claims.reasoning: Collapse is excluded (I.PERILS.A.2.a) except as provided by the Collapse additional coverage, which covers abrupt collapse caused by a Coverage C peril (I.ADD.8.b). Weight of ice, snow or sleet is one (I.PERILS.C.11). The workshop is an other structure (I.B.1).

claims.lossDescription: The water heater tank has corroded and is leaking slowly. A plumber says it must be replaced.
claims.question: Is the cost to replace the water heater covered?
claims.reasoning: Version 2 includes equipment breakdown, but it does not cover corrosion or gradual deterioration unless it results in a sudden breakdown (PS-EB/5); a slow leak is not sudden. The base form excludes corrosion (I.PERILS.A.2.g.3).

claims.lossDescription: The furnace stopped working.
claims.question: Is the furnace repair covered?
claims.reasoning: Equipment breakdown covers a sudden failure that causes physical damage (PS-EB/2) but not wear, corrosion, or a malfunction needing only adjustment (PS-EB/5). Why the furnace stopped is not known.

claims.lossDescription: The insureds' son set off fireworks in the back yard and one landed on the neighbor's roof, burning a section of shingles.
claims.question: Is the son covered for the damage to the neighbor's roof?
claims.reasoning: Coverage E applies if the damage was accidental (II.E) but not if it was expected or intended (II.EXCL.5); whether the son aimed at the roof, and his liability, are not established.

claims.lossDescription: Children playing indoors knocked a hole through a drywall partition with a hockey stick.
claims.question: Is the damage to the wall covered?
claims.reasoning: Under the named perils form, the dwelling is covered only for the listed perils (I.PERILS.0). Accidental damage by the occupants is not one of them.

claims.lossDescription: A fire destroyed half of the dwelling. The city requires the rebuilt part to meet current building code, which adds $40,000 for wiring, sprinklers and structural work.
claims.question: Is the $40,000 of code upgrade cost covered?
claims.reasoning: Fire is a listed peril (I.PERILS.1). The base form pays code costs up to 10% of Coverage A, $21,000 (I.ADD.11); the endorsement raises that to 25% (PS-OL/1, Declarations), $52,500, which covers the full $40,000.

claims.lossDescription: A fire destroyed half of the dwelling. Because of historic-district rules, the rebuilt house will be worth less than before.
claims.question: Is the loss in the dwelling's market value covered?
claims.reasoning: The Ordinance or Law coverage excludes loss in value of a building due to ordinance or law (I.ADD.11), and the endorsement keeps that exclusion (PS-OL/2).

claims.lossDescription: An electrician says the 1931 wiring does not meet current code and must be replaced. Nothing has been damaged.
claims.question: Is the rewiring covered?
claims.reasoning: There is no loss caused by a listed peril (I.PERILS.0). Ordinance or Law coverage applies only to parts damaged by a peril insured against (I.ADD.11), and ordinance or law is otherwise excluded (I.EXCL.1).

claims.lossDescription: During an ordinary rain, the old shingles leaked and water stained the plaster ceiling of an upstairs room. There was no wind damage.
claims.question: Is the ceiling damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Rain damage to the inside of a building is covered under windstorm only when wind first makes an opening (I.PERILS.2), and a leak from worn shingles is not a listed peril (I.PERILS.0).

claims.lossDescription: Raccoons got into the attic and chewed through electrical wiring and insulation.
claims.question: Is the damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Damage by animals is not among the listed perils (I.PERILS.0).

claims.lossDescription: A neighbor's teenager lost control of a car and drove through the insured's wooden fence.
claims.question: Is the fence damage covered?
claims.reasoning: The fence is an other structure (I.B.1). Vehicles is a listed peril; its limitation applies only to vehicles owned or operated by a resident of the residence premises (I.PERILS.6).

claims.lossDescription: The city sewer backed up through the basement floor drain during a storm, leaving sewage on the basement floor.
claims.question: Is the basement damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Water or waterborne material that backs up through sewers or drains is excluded (I.EXCL.3.b), and HO-1004 has no water backup endorsement.

claims.lossDescription: A windstorm damaged the roof. The insured is deciding whether to file a claim.
claims.question: Will the insured's premium go up if they file this claim?
claims.reasoning: The policy does not address future premiums; that is a matter of the insurer's rating rules, not policy wording.

claims.lossDescription: Mold is growing on the basement walls.
claims.question: Is the mold damage covered?
claims.reasoning: Under named perils, mold is covered only as part of an accidental discharge from plumbing when hidden in walls, floors or ceilings (I.PERILS.12). Other causes, such as humidity or ground water, are not listed perils (I.PERILS.0). The cause is not known.

claims.lossDescription: The insured's scheduled engagement ring was stolen from a locker at the gym.
claims.question: Is the theft of the ring covered?
claims.reasoning: The ring is scheduled at $12,000 (Declarations) and covered against direct physical loss anywhere in the world (PS-SP/1).

claims.lossDescription: The diamond fell out of the insured's scheduled engagement ring at some point during the day. The insured does not know where or when.
claims.question: Is the lost diamond covered?
claims.reasoning: Scheduled property is covered for mysterious disappearance; the insured need not show theft (PS-SP/2). The ring is scheduled (Declarations), and coverage is against direct physical loss (PS-SP/1).

claims.lossDescription: An unscheduled gold bracelet worth $5,000 went missing at a concert. There is no sign it was stolen.
claims.question: Is the bracelet covered?
claims.reasoning: Only scheduled items get mysterious disappearance coverage. The bracelet is under Coverage C, which covers listed perils only (I.PERILS.C.0); theft requires that the property was likely stolen (I.PERILS.C.9).

claims.lossDescription: Burglars took the insured's scheduled wristwatch ($6,500) and a pair of unscheduled diamond earrings ($4,000).
claims.question: Is the full value of the wristwatch covered?
claims.reasoning: The watch is scheduled at $6,500 (Declarations), covered by the endorsement (PS-SP/1), and the $1,500 theft limit on jewelry does not apply to scheduled property (PS-SP/3).

claims.lossDescription: Burglars took the insured's scheduled wristwatch ($6,500) and a pair of unscheduled diamond earrings ($4,000).
claims.question: Are the earrings covered for more than $1,500?
claims.reasoning: The earrings are not scheduled, so they fall under Coverage C, where theft of jewelry is limited to $1,500 per loss (I.C.3.e).

claims.lossDescription: Tree roots cracked the sewer line between the house and the street, on the insured's property. Excavating and replacing it costs $7,500.
claims.question: Is the sewer line repair covered?
claims.reasoning: The sewer line is a service line (PS-SL/1); a break caused by tree roots is a service line failure (PS-SL/2); the endorsement pays up to $10,000 including excavation, less a $500 deductible (PS-SL/3).

claims.lossDescription: A landscaper hired by the insured dug into the underground water line and broke it.
claims.question: Is the water line repair covered?
claims.reasoning: Service line coverage excludes damage caused by excavation done by an insured or anyone on an insured's behalf (PS-SL/4).

claims.lossDescription: The insured's scheduled pearl necklace was damaged while a jeweler was restringing it.
claims.question: Is the damage to the necklace covered?
claims.reasoning: Scheduled property is not covered for loss caused by repairing or restoring (PS-SP/4).

claims.lossDescription: The insured bought diamond earrings for $2,800 on 2026-09-01 and had not yet reported them to the insurer. They were stolen on 2026-09-12.
claims.question: Are the new earrings covered for their full cost?
claims.reasoning: Newly acquired jewelry is covered for 30 days for its actual cost, up to 25% of the jewelry class ($5,375) or $10,000, whichever is less (PS-SP/6). The theft was 11 days after purchase.

claims.lossDescription: The insured's scheduled engagement ring is missing. The insured thinks the cleaner may have taken it but has no proof.
claims.question: Is the missing ring covered?
claims.reasoning: The policy settles this even though the facts are uncertain: scheduled property is covered whether it was stolen (PS-SP/1) or simply disappeared (PS-SP/2).

claims.lossDescription: Hail dented the roof. No estimate has been made yet.
claims.question: Will the insurer pay anything for the roof?
claims.reasoning: Hail damage is covered, but the insurer pays only the amount above the $2,000 deductible (I.COND.2, Declarations). Without an estimate, whether the loss exceeds the deductible is unknown.

claims.lossDescription: A kiln overheated in the garage pottery studio and the fire damaged the garage structure.
claims.question: Is the damage to the garage covered?
claims.reasoning: Other structures used for a business are not covered (I.B.4), but the home business endorsement removes that limitation for the structure housing the declared home business (PS-HB/3). Fire is a listed peril (I.PERILS.1).

claims.lossDescription: A student in a pottery class at the garage studio was burned by the kiln fire and is suing.
claims.question: Is the insured covered for the student's suit?
claims.reasoning: The business exclusion does not apply to injury arising out of the declared home business, including injury to customers on the residence premises (PS-HB/7), so Coverage E applies (II.E).

claims.lossDescription: Dana Whitfield also sells antiques online, earning about $20,000 a year; this is not the declared home business. Antiques worth $6,000 stored in the dwelling were stolen.
claims.question: Is the theft of the antiques covered for their full value?
claims.reasoning: Selling antiques for $20,000 a year is a business under the definition (DEF.6.b). The endorsement covers only the declared home business (PS-HB/2), so the antiques are business property subject to the $2,500 on-premises limit (I.C.3.h).

claims.lossDescription: A customer collecting an antique from Dana Whitfield's online antiques business tripped on the driveway and broke an ankle. The antiques business is not the declared home business.
claims.question: Is the customer's injury covered under the liability coverages?
claims.reasoning: The antiques business is a business (DEF.6.b) but not the declared home business, which is all the endorsement covers (PS-HB/2). Injury arising out of a business is excluded from Coverages E and F (II.EXCL.6.a).

claims.lossDescription: The tenant in the upper unit had a laptop stolen from her apartment.
claims.question: Is the tenant's laptop covered by this policy?
claims.reasoning: Coverage C covers property of insureds (I.C.1); the tenant is not an insured, and property of tenants is not covered (I.C.4.e).

claims.lossDescription: A supply pipe burst in the tenant's upper unit. Water came through the floor and damaged the ceiling of Dana Whitfield's ground-floor unit.
claims.question: Is the damage to the ground-floor ceiling covered?
claims.reasoning: The two-family dwelling is the covered dwelling (I.A.1), and accidental discharge of water from a plumbing system is a listed peril (I.PERILS.12).

claims.lossDescription: A casserole dish sold by Whitfield Clayworks cracked in a customer's oven and the customer was burned.
claims.question: Is Dana Whitfield covered for the customer's injury?
claims.reasoning: Injury arising out of products the home business sells is covered (PS-HB/7), subject to the products aggregate (PS-HB/9), under Coverage E (II.E). The off-premises limitation in PS-HB/8 does not apply to products sold.

claims.lossDescription: Dana Whitfield taught a pottery class at a community center. A student was injured when Dana dropped a box of equipment.
claims.question: Is the student's injury covered?
claims.reasoning: Home business liability coverage does not extend to activities conducted away from the residence premises other than products sold (PS-HB/8).

claims.lossDescription: Dana Whitfield cares for her sister's young son at home on weekdays, for pay. The child fell from a chair and was injured.
claims.question: Is Dana covered for the child's injury?
claims.reasoning: Providing home day care to a relative is not a business under the definition (DEF.6.c), so the business exclusion does not apply and Coverage E covers the injury (II.E).

claims.lossDescription: Whitfield Clayworks' part-time employee broke a wrist slipping on clay in the studio.
claims.question: Is the employee's injury covered under the liability coverages?
claims.reasoning: Home business liability coverage excludes injury to an employee in the course of employment (PS-HB/8); such injuries fall under workers' compensation (II.EXCL.16).

claims.lossDescription: Wind blew in a studio window and rain soaked $12,000 of finished pottery awaiting sale.
claims.question: Is the pottery inventory covered?
claims.reasoning: Wind made an opening, so rain damage inside is covered under windstorm (I.PERILS.2). Home business inventory held for sale is covered up to $10,000 per loss (PS-HB/5).

claims.lossDescription: A fraudster used Dana Whitfield's identity to open a business line of credit in the name of Whitfield Clayworks. Dana incurred $900 of expenses restoring the business's credit.
claims.question: Are the expenses covered by the identity fraud endorsement?
claims.reasoning: Identity fraud expense coverage excludes expenses arising out of a business of an insured (PS-ID/4).

claims.lossDescription: During a storm, a tree from the neighbor's yard fell on Dana Whitfield's fence.
claims.question: Can Dana's insurer recover its payment from the neighbor?
claims.reasoning: The insurer may take over the insured's right of recovery (GEN.6), but whether the neighbor is liable depends on facts the policy does not settle, such as whether the neighbor knew the tree was unsound.

claims.lossDescription: Fire damaged the garage studio. Repairs have not started.
claims.question: How long will the repairs take?
claims.reasoning: The policy does not address repair schedules.

claims.lossDescription: The tenant says water leaking from Dana Whitfield's unit damaged the tenant's belongings.
claims.question: Will this policy pay for the tenant's belongings?
claims.reasoning: Tenants' property is not covered under Section I (I.C.4.e). Coverage E would pay only if Dana is legally liable for the leak (II.E), which depends on its cause.

claims.lossDescription: It poured all night and dirty water came gushing up out of the hole in my basement floor. The carpet's ruined and the bottom of the walls are soaked.
claims.question: Am I covered for the basement?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-003, in the claimant's own words. Water that backs up through sewers or drains is excluded by I.EXCL.3.b. HO-1001 has no water backup endorsement.

claims.lossDescription: It poured all night and dirty water came gushing up out of the hole in my basement floor. The carpet's ruined and the bottom of the walls are soaked.
claims.question: Am I covered for the basement?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-024, in the claimant's own words. The water backup endorsement covers water that backs up through drains (PS-WB/1) and deletes exclusion 3.b for that coverage (PS-WB/2), up to the $10,000 Water Backup limit (PS-WB/5, Declarations).

claims.lossDescription: The power went out in the storm and the pump in the pit in my basement stopped. By morning the whole floor was under water.
claims.question: Will insurance pay for this?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-026, in the claimant's own words. Overflow from a sump is covered by the endorsement (PS-WB/1), and the off-premises power failure exclusion does not apply when the overflow results from loss of power to a sump pump (PS-WB/3).

claims.lossDescription: Heater quit on us in February; the repair guy says a motor in it fried. He wants $3,200.
claims.question: Do I have to pay for this myself?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-035, in the claimant's own words. On 2026-02-10 version 1 is in force, without equipment breakdown coverage. Loss caused by mechanical breakdown is not insured (I.PERILS.A.2.g.2).

claims.lossDescription: Heater quit on us in October; the repair guy says a motor in it fried. He wants $3,200.
claims.question: Do I have to pay for this myself?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-036, in the claimant's own words. On 2026-10-25 version 2 is in force and includes equipment breakdown. A burned-out motor is a sudden mechanical breakdown of covered equipment (PS-EB/1, PS-EB/2), and the mechanical breakdown exclusion does not apply to this coverage (PS-EB/4).

claims.lossDescription: My kids were horsing around with a hockey stick and smashed a hole in the wall.
claims.question: Can I claim the wall?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-019, in the claimant's own words. Under the open perils form, the dwelling is covered for any direct physical loss not excluded (I.PERILS.A.1). Accidental damage is not excluded.

claims.lossDescription: My kids were horsing around with a hockey stick and smashed a hole in the wall.
claims.question: Can I claim the wall?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-048, in the claimant's own words. Under the named perils form, the dwelling is covered only for the listed perils (I.PERILS.0). Accidental damage by the occupants is not one of them.

claims.lossDescription: I looked down and the stone was just gone from my engagement ring. No idea where it fell out.
claims.question: Is my ring stone covered?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-059, in the claimant's own words. Scheduled property is covered for mysterious disappearance; the insured need not show theft (PS-SP/2). The ring is scheduled (Declarations), and coverage is against direct physical loss (PS-SP/1).

claims.lossDescription: Toilets kept backing up; the plumber ran a camera and says roots busted the pipe out to the street. Have to dig up the yard.
claims.question: Will my policy pay for the dig and the pipe?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-063, in the claimant's own words. The sewer line is a service line (PS-SL/1); a break caused by tree roots is a service line failure (PS-SL/2); the endorsement pays up to $10,000 including excavation, less a $500 deductible (PS-SL/3).

claims.lossDescription: Someone broke in and took the old furniture and lamps I resell on the internet, about $6,000 worth. It's my side hustle, not the pottery.
claims.question: Am I getting the whole $6,000?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-071, in the claimant's own words. Selling antiques for $20,000 a year is a business under the definition (DEF.6.b). The endorsement covers only the declared home business (PS-HB/2), so the antiques are business property subject to the $2,500 on-premises limit (I.C.3.h).

claims.lossDescription: My boy cuts grass around the block for pocket money and a rock flew out of the mower and hit the neighbor in the eye.
claims.question: Are we covered if they come after us?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-013, in the claimant's own words. The son is an insured as a resident relative. His mowing is not a business under the definition, because no insured earned more than $3,000 from it (DEF.6.c); even if it were, the business exclusion does not apply to an insured under 21 in an occasional self-employed business with no employees (II.EXCL.6.c).

claims.lossDescription: We got back from two weeks away and somebody had tagged our garage door with spray paint.
claims.question: Is this covered?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-015, in the claimant's own words. The vandalism limitation in I.PERILS.A.2.e applies only when the dwelling has been vacant for more than 60 days. A furnished house whose occupants are temporarily away is unoccupied, not vacant (DEF.16), so the garage (I.B.1) is covered.

claims.lossDescription: Lightning hit right next to the house and fried the TV and the computer.
claims.question: Can I get new ones through insurance?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-017, in the claimant's own words. Lightning is a Coverage C peril (I.PERILS.C.1). The exclusion of electronic components applies only to the peril of artificially generated electrical current (I.PERILS.C.15), and lightning is not artificially generated.

claims.lossDescription: All that snow and the roof of my shop out back just fell in.
claims.question: Is the shop covered?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-044, in the claimant's own words. Collapse is excluded (I.PERILS.A.2.a) except as provided by the Collapse additional coverage, which covers abrupt collapse caused by a Coverage C peril (I.ADD.8.b). Weight of ice, snow or sleet is one (I.PERILS.C.11). The workshop is an other structure (I.B.1).

claims.lossDescription: After the fire the city says we have to bring everything up to today's code when we rebuild. That's another $40,000.
claims.question: Does insurance pay the extra $40,000?
claims.reasoning: Same facts as GS-049, in the claimant's own words. Fire is a listed peril (I.PERILS.1). The base form pays code costs up to 10% of Coverage A, $21,000 (I.ADD.11); the endorsement raises that to 25% (PS-OL/1, Declarations), $52,500, which covers the full $40,000.
